summary: ModToken is a 34-line ERC20 over the shared ERC20Base: it mints `initialSupply` to the deployer in the constructor, exposes an owner-only `mint()` that is gated by an immutable-in-practice `mintable` flag, and lets anyone burn their own balance. The token logic itself is sound (no hooks, no reentrancy surface, unchecked math is invariant-protected, transfers revert rather than return false), so a fixed-supply deployment (`mintable_=false`, the catalog default) is safe to use as-is. The worst thing found is the intended-but-total power of `mint()` when `mintable_=true`: the owner can print unlimited supply and use it to drain any AMM, lending pool, CDP, PSM or staking block wired to this asset, and `mintable` can only be revoked by renouncing ownership. Two composition issues matter for deployers: the token has no vote checkpoints, so wiring it as ModGovernor's `votes` allows transfer-and-revote (and, with a flashlender on the same asset, flash voting), and transfers to address(0) are accepted without reducing `totalSupply`.

findings.title: Owner mint is unbounded and drains every downstream block when mintable_=true
findings.detail: With `mintable_=true` the owner can call `mint(to, amount)` for any amount with no cap, rate limit, timelock or event beyond Transfer. Every catalog block that takes this token on an `erc20` port prices it by balance: the AMM and StableSwap swap it against the other reserve, the lending pool and CDP accept it as collateral, the PSM swaps it for the stable, staking/gauge blocks weight rewards by stake. Freshly minted supply therefore converts directly into the other side of any pool it is wired into. By default `owner_` resolves to the deploying wallet (`$input:governor|$owner`), i.e. a single EOA holds the lever unless a governor/timelock is wired. There is also no way to turn `mintable` off short of `setOwner(address(0))`, so a deployer who wants a temporary bootstrap mint cannot later close it while keeping ownership.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy ModToken with mintable_=true, owner = deployer EOA. 2. Wire it as token0 of ModAMM against a real asset (e.g. USDC) and let LPs add liquidity, or as `collateral` of ModLendingPool with a ModFixedOracle price. 3. Owner calls mint(owner, 1e30). 4. Owner swaps the minted tokens into the AMM, taking essentially the entire token1 reserve; or deposits them as collateral and borrows the whole debtAsset reserve. LPs / lenders are left holding worthless inflated supply.
findings.recommendation: Keep `mintable_=false` for any token that will back real value. If minting is needed, add a hard `cap` checked in mint(), a `disableMint()` (or `renounceMinting()`) that flips `mintable` to false permanently without giving up ownership, and wire the `governor` port to a ModTimelock/ModGovernor so mints are visible and delayed. Emit a dedicated Mint event.

findings.title: No vote checkpoints: wired as ModGovernor `votes`, balances can be moved and re-voted, flash-voted, and quorum shifts live
findings.where: ERC20Base.transfer()/transferFrom() common.sol L78-L91, burn() L31-L33, mint() L26-L29; consumer governor.sol L106-L108, L129, L151
findings.detail: ModToken is a plain balance token with no snapshotting or delegation checkpoints. ModGovernor reads `votes.balanceOf(msg.sender)` at castVote time and `votes.totalSupply()` for quorum, and de-duplicates only per address (`hasVoted[id][msg.sender]`). Because the token freely transfers, one balance can vote from N addresses. If a ModFlashLender is deployed over the same token, a voter can borrow the reserve, vote, and repay in one transaction. Public `burn()` lets anyone lower quorum mid-vote, and the owner's `mint()` raises it (or mints votes to itself). The root defect is in the governor's live-balance reads, but the token is what the catalog offers as the governance asset, so deployers hit this the moment they draw the token -> governor edge.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy token (fixed supply), ModGovernor with votes=token, quorumBps=1000. 2. Attacker holds 1,000 tokens in address A. 3. A.castVote(id, true) -> +1,000 for. 4. A.transfer(B, 1000); B.castVote(id, true) -> +1,000 for. 5. Repeat across 50 fresh addresses in one block: 50,000 votes from 1,000 tokens, clearing quorum and majority. Variant: with a ModFlashLender on the token, flashLoan(reserve) -> castVote -> repay in the callback.
findings.recommendation: For governance use, mint an ERC20Votes-style token (checkpointed `getPastVotes`, delegation) or have ModGovernor snapshot balances/totalSupply at proposal start. At minimum, do not deploy a ModFlashLender over the governance token and set a meaningful votingDelay so transfers after proposal are visible.

findings.title: Ownership transfer is single-step with no zero check; it is the only way to revoke minting
findings.detail: `setOwner` assigns any address immediately, with no acceptance step and no zero-address guard. On a mintable token the owner role is exactly the unlimited mint key (TOKEN-1), so a typo hands that key to an unknown address irrevocably, and a fat-fingered zero renounces it. Renouncing is also the *only* way to end minting, which pushes deployers toward the risky call instead of a dedicated flag.
findings.exploit: 1. Mintable token owned by EOA. 2. Owner calls setOwner(0x...typo). 3. Whoever controls that address (or nobody) now holds unbounded mint; the original owner cannot recover. Conversely, a wired ModGovernor proposal that mistakenly targets setOwner(governorTypo) permanently detaches the token from governance.
findings.recommendation: Use a two-step transfer (pendingOwner + acceptOwner). Add an explicit `disableMint()` so revoking mint does not require renouncing. If a deployer does intend to renounce, call setOwner(address(0)) deliberately and verify `owner()` afterwards.

findings.title: Transfers to address(0) succeed and leave totalSupply overstated
findings.detail: `_move` does not reject `to == address(0)`. Tokens sent there are unrecoverable but remain counted in `totalSupply` and in `balanceOf(0)`. Anything that treats `totalSupply` as circulating supply — ModGovernor's quorum (`votes.totalSupply() * quorumBps`), off-chain dashboards, share-price maths in blocks that compare against supply — drifts upward. Users who expect the standard ERC20 revert on zero-address transfers get a silent loss instead.
findings.exploit: 1. User (or an integrating contract with an uninitialised `to`) calls transfer(address(0), 1e24). 2. Call returns true; tokens are gone; totalSupply unchanged. 3. In a wired governor, quorum now includes 1e24 dead votes that can never be cast, making proposals harder to pass than the deployer configured.
findings.recommendation: Add `require(to != address(0), "ZERO_TO")` in `_move` (and by extension transfer/transferFrom); use `burn()` for intentional destruction so totalSupply stays accurate.

findings.title: approve() is exposed to the classic allowance front-running race
findings.detail: Allowance is overwritten unconditionally, so changing a non-zero allowance to another non-zero value lets the spender consume both the old and the new amounts by front-running. No increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance helpers are offered.
findings.exploit: 1. Alice approves Bob 100. 2. Alice broadcasts approve(Bob, 50). 3. Bob sees it in the mempool, front-runs transferFrom(Alice, Bob, 100), then after Alice's tx lands spends a further 50. Bob moved 150 against an intended 50.
findings.recommendation: Add increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance, or document that integrators should set allowance to 0 before a new non-zero value. Catalog blocks pull via transferFrom with exact amounts, so the risk is with human wallets, not block-to-block wiring.

findings.title: decimals_ is not validated; values above 18 break downstream blocks at deploy time
findings.where: constructor L11-L24, ERC20Base constructor common.sol L66-L70; consumers stableswap.sol L55-L56, psm.sol L49
findings.detail: Any uint8 is accepted. ModStableSwap computes `10 ** (18 - decimals())`, which reverts on underflow for decimals > 18, and ModPSM's `10 ** decimals()` plus the planner's `scale: decimals_` for `initialSupply` overflow for very large values. The token itself works with any decimals; the failure is a revert (or an absurd initial supply) when the graph is deployed, not a fund loss.
findings.exploit: 1. Set decimals_=24, initialSupply=1000000. 2. Wire the token as coin0 of a ModStableSwap. 3. The StableSwap constructor reverts (`18 - 24` underflows), so the deployment plan fails after the token has already been created.
findings.recommendation: Keep decimals at 18 (or 6/8 to mirror the paired asset). Consider `require(decimals_ <= 18)` in the constructor, or have the planner enforce it, so the catalog's arithmetic assumptions hold.

safe_use: Leave `Owner can mint more` (mintable_) OFF for any token that will back real value in an AMM, lending, CDP, PSM or staking block; fixed-supply is the safe default and is what the catalog ships.
If you must enable minting, wire the `governor` port to a ModTimelock or ModGovernor before adding liquidity anywhere, so every mint is a delayed, public proposal rather than one EOA's signature.
To permanently end minting on a mintable token, call setOwner(address(0)) and verify owner() == 0 afterwards; there is no separate disable switch, and setOwner is single-step with no undo.

Do not use this token as ModGovernor `votes` for anything with real stakes: it has no checkpoints, so balances can be moved and re-voted or flash-borrowed. Never deploy a ModFlashLender over a governance token.
Keep decimals_ at 18 (or matching the asset it will be paired with); values above 18 make StableSwap/PSM constructors revert.
Transfers to address(0) do not revert and do not reduce totalSupply; use burn() for intentional destruction and double-check recipient addresses in wallets.

initialSupply is minted to the deploying wallet ($owner) at construction; when the governor port is wired, ownership goes to the governor but the supply still lands in your wallet, so plan the distribution (vesting, airdrop, treasury) explicitly.
